How property tax works in New Mexico

Counties run property tax in New Mexico, with oversight from the state Taxation and Revenue Department. Your county assessor decides the value and your county treasurer collects the money. The department's Property Tax Division backs up the counties and handles collection on accounts that stay delinquent for years.

Of the state's 33 counties, only some hold delinquent auctions in a given year. Rates apply to no more than thirty-three and one-third percent of value under the constitution, so the net taxable value on your notice is only a fraction of market value. The Property Tax Code adds a separate limit on yearly increases for homes, covered below.

A seller mostly deals with four moments: the spring notice of valuation, the two installments, the January 1 lien date and the closing statement that settles the balance.

Due dates and amounts

A handful of figures cover most homeowners.

Property tax dates, limits and exemptions
TopicRuleStatute
Notice of valuationMailed by the assessor around April 1NMSA 7-38-20
Protest petitionFiled with the assessor, generally thirty days after the notice is mailedNMSA 7-38-24
Tax installmentsNovember 10 and April 10, in two equal installments for bills of $10 or moreNMSA 7-38-38
Interest on unpaid taxOne percent a month, starting thirty days after the due dateNMSA 7-38-49
Tax lienAttaches to real property from January 1 of the tax yearNMSA 7-38-48
Residential value limitHigher of 103 percent of prior year value or 106.1 percent of value two years backNMSA 7-36-21.2
Head of family exemptionUp to $2,000 of taxable valueNMSA 7-37-4
Veteran exemption$10,000, adjusted annually for inflationState announcement, Aug. 2026

Interest doesn't run on interest or on penalties, and it accrues even while a protest is pending. If the protest succeeds, interest is computed on the unpaid tax finally found due.

The cap on increases and what resets it

In any one year, a home's taxable value is held to the greater of 103 percent of last year's value or 106.1 percent of the value two years back. Long-time owners are shielded from sudden market jumps this way.

The limit stops applying for a property's first valued year, for physical improvements (solar installations excepted), for a change in use or zoning, and for the year following a change of ownership. After a sale the county sets the house at current and correct value, as described in Section 7-36-21.2.

Certain transfers don't count as a change of ownership: between spouses, into a revocable trust for the owner, spouse or child, and to a child who lives there as a principal residence. Moving a house between a person and their own LLC does count, per a 2019 Court of Appeals decision.

Your bill and the buyer's can look very different, so base the buyer's carrying costs on the reset value.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Mexico house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Exemptions that lower a tax bill

Head of family takes up to $2,000 off taxable value for qualifying residents, and the veteran exemption now takes $10,000. Each comes off taxable value on the way to net taxable value.

  • Head of family: open to a married person, a widow or widower, a head of household supporting a relative, a single person, or a condo association member who pays tax through the association. One person per household qualifies, and you can claim it in only one county each year.
  • Veteran: the standard amount rose from $4,000 to $10,000. A qualifying veteran obtains a certificate of eligibility from the state department of veteran services and files it with the county assessor.
  • Disabled veteran: from 2026, a partially disabled veteran can receive a prorated exemption based on disability rating.
  • Valuation freeze: a single-family home that an owner aged 65 or older, or disabled, lives in stays at its assessed value from the year the owner qualifies, provided prior-year modified gross income is $35,000 or less as adjusted for inflation.

Under Section 7-38-17, you claim an exemption within thirty days of the mailed notice of valuation, and it then renews itself while nothing changes. Report any change in eligibility or ownership to the assessor by the end of the next February. Knowingly filing a false claim is a misdemeanor.

How to protest a valuation

Send a written petition to the county assessor, usually within thirty days of the date the valuation notice was mailed. State your name, describe the property, explain why the value looks wrong and give the value you think is right.

An informal conference with the assessor may come first, and many protests end there. Otherwise a three-member county valuation protests board takes the case. It works apart from the assessor and seats two county residents named by the commission plus an appraisal officer from the state Property Tax Division.

  • The assessor sets the hearing and mails notice at least fifteen days ahead. Discovery requests can take thirty days to answer, so prepare early.
  • The assessor's number starts out presumed correct, and you carry the burden of presenting evidence against it.
  • Witnesses testify under oath and the hearing is recorded word for word.
  • A written order follows within thirty days of the hearing, and every protest is supposed to be decided within 180 days of filing.
  • Appeal to district court within thirty days of the order.

There's a second route after you pay. An owner who pays before the delinquency date can contest value, classification or a denied exemption through a refund claim in district court, under Section 7-38-39.

What happens when property tax goes unpaid?

Interest on unpaid tax runs at one percent a month once thirty days pass after the due date, and the lien remains until the bill is paid. It ranks ahead of every other interest, perfected or not, and exists by operation of law with no recorded notice needed.

The state's Delinquent Property Tax Bureau steps in after the third full year of delinquency. Title research is finished first, then sales happen each year, typically at the county courthouse, and not every one of the 33 counties has a sale annually.

Rules worth knowing if an auction is coming:

  • The opening bid equals taxes, penalty, interest and costs owed.
  • The buyer gets a tax deed that works like a quitclaim deed: as is, with no title warranty.
  • Only the tax lien is wiped out. Other liens survive.
  • Former owners get no redemption right in New Mexico, just two years to challenge the sale in court under Section 7-38-70.
  • If the IRS holds a lien, a 120-day federal redemption period may apply.
  • Under Section 7-38-53, a county treasurer can seize and sell a mobile home over delinquent tax.

Since nothing can be redeemed afterward, selling ahead of the auction is the main way to keep equity.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Mexico houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

Back tax can come out of your sale proceeds at closing, since the first lien stays with the property until paid. Steps:

  • Get the current balance with interest from the county treasurer before listing.
  • See whether a head of family or veteran exemption was ever claimed. The window is thirty days from the mailed notice of valuation.
  • If a sale ends an exemption, tell the assessor by the end of the following February.
  • Decide whether to keep any pending protest alive, remembering that interest runs while it's pending.
  • Have the title company quote a payoff covering the November and April installments for the closing year.

Cash Home Buyers purchases New Mexico houses as they are, back taxes included, and the payoff is handled on the closing statement. We aren't tax advisors, so confirm balances with the treasurer or call the Property Tax Division at (505) 827-0883.

Frequently asked questions

When are New Mexico property taxes due?

Two equal installments on November 10 and April 10 for bills of $10 or more. An unpaid installment starts earning one percent monthly interest thirty days after its due date.

How long do I have to protest my New Mexico property valuation?

Generally thirty days from the mailing of the notice of valuation. You petition the county assessor, who sets a hearing before the county valuation protests board.

Does New Mexico cap how much my property tax value can rise?

Yes, on residential property. Value can't climb past the greater of 103 percent of last year or 106.1 percent of two years back, and the cap resets when ownership changes.

Can I get my house back after a New Mexico tax auction?

No, there's no redemption right. You have two years to challenge the sale in court under Section 7-38-70, and a 120-day federal period applies if the IRS holds a lien.

What is the New Mexico veteran property tax exemption?

The standard exemption for a veteran who owns property rose from $4,000 to $10,000 and adjusts yearly for inflation. Get a certificate of eligibility from the state department of veteran services and file it with the county assessor.

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Mexico Homestead Exemption sale
  • Turn the New Mexico Homestead Exemption offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New Mexico House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in New Mexico?
We buy New Mexico houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

What the New Mexico homestead exemption is

The New Mexico homestead exemption is a creditor protection rule in Section 42-10-9 NMSA 1978. It shields part of the value of your primary residence from a judgment creditor, from a bankruptcy trustee and from probate administrators.

Many owners confuse it with property tax relief, but the two are separate. This page covers the creditor protection first, then the tax exemptions that sometimes share the "homestead" label, because the difference matters when you decide how and when to sell.

A person has a homestead exemption in a domicile or land the person owns and uses as a primary residence. The protection runs against attachment, execution or foreclosure by a judgment creditor. It does not protect the property against a mortgage you signed.

How much is the exemption?

The current amount is $150,000, or $300,000 in one situation: the claimant's spouse died within two years before the claim and could have claimed the exemption had they lived. The amount comes from the 2023 amendment, which took effect July 1, 2023 and applies to actions filed on or after that date.

The number has moved a lot. It was $20,000 before 1993, rose to $30,000 with the 1993 amendment, and rose to $60,000 effective June 15, 2007. From then until mid 2023 each joint owner of a jointly owned homestead had a separate $60,000.

An older court case holds that a legislative increase cannot be claimed against a judgment lien that attached before the increase took effect. If a lien is old, the amount in force when it attached can matter.

What counts as a domicile

A domicile is any shelter or dwelling you use as a primary residence. A mobile home, trailer, recreational vehicle or outbuilding can qualify, even if the dwelling does not meet building or housing regulations.

The statute is to be construed liberally in favor of the person claiming it. Court decisions show how that plays out.

  • An equitable owner, such as a buyer under a contract, can claim the exemption, not only the holder of a recorded deed.
  • A debtor who held a life estate in her residence was allowed to claim it in a 2020 federal bankruptcy decision.
  • A debtor with an undivided quarter interest in an inherited house still titled in his deceased parents' names was allowed to claim it in another 2020 bankruptcy decision, because title passes to heirs at death under the Uniform Probate Code.
  • A trailer used as a dwelling qualified, and two rental trailers on the same lot did not defeat the claim.
  • A debtor who moved out because creditors had taken judgments did not abandon the homestead when she intended to return.

These rulings turned on their own facts. They show direction, not a guarantee for your situation.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Mexico house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What the exemption does not protect

The exemption does not apply to garnishment or to properly perfected liens of secured creditors, so a recorded mortgage or deed of trust is untouched by it. Subsection E of the statute says so directly.

Other limits come up often in the cases.

  • A mortgage can waive the exemption. An old Supreme Court case holds that an owner can give it up by mortgage or other act.
  • Sale proceeds are a gray area. A 1991 bankruptcy decision held that when an owner voluntarily sells the homestead, the proceeds are not exempt.
  • Intentional damage to the property can carry an equitable lien against the exemption, as in a foreclosure where the debtor sabotaged the house.
  • Property tax is a first lien on real property from January 1 of the tax year under Section 7-38-48, ahead of other interests, and the homestead exemption protects against judgment creditors, not against that lien.

A judgment lien still attaches to a home. A 2019 bankruptcy decision held that a judgment lien encumbers the homestead and can be avoided to the extent it impairs the exemption. The exemption limits what a creditor can collect. It does not keep the lien from showing up on title.

How to claim it

You claim the exemption in the proceeding where a creditor is trying to collect, using the court forms for that proceeding. Rule 4-803 NMRA covers a claim of exemptions on execution, and Rule 4-808A covers the notice of the right to claim exemptions.

In a foreclosure, an answer is the place to assert it. A 1998 Court of Appeals decision allowed a mortgagor to keep the exemption against a junior judgment lien because she raised it in her answer and obtained court approval of a sale to a third party while the case was pending. An older Supreme Court decision denied the exemption to mortgagors who failed to assert it against junior lienholders in their answers.

Because court forms can lag behind a statute change, have an attorney confirm the current dollar amount before you rely on a number.

Homestead exemption versus property tax exemptions

The property tax exemptions are a different set of rules, and they reduce a county tax bill instead of protecting equity from creditors. Three come up most often.

County property tax programs for homeowners
ProgramWhat it doesWho it covers
Head of family exemption (7-37-4)Up to $2,000 off the taxable value of residential propertyA New Mexico resident who is a married person, widow or widower, head of household supporting a related person, single person or condominium association member; one claim per household and one county per year
Veteran exemptionRaised from $4,000 to $10,000, adjusted annually for inflationVeteran owners; a certificate of eligibility from the state is filed with the county assessor
Valuation freeze (7-36-21.3)Caps the assessed value of a single-family homeOwner-occupants aged 65 or older, or disabled, whose prior-year modified gross income did not exceed $35,000 as adjusted for inflation

Under Section 7-38-17, head of family and veteran exemptions continue automatically once allowed if nothing changes. A first claim is due within thirty days after the assessor mails the notice of valuation. If you lose eligibility, including by selling, you must tell the county assessor by the last day of February of the following year. A knowing false claim is a misdemeanor with a fine up to $1,000.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Mexico houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

What happens to your tax benefits when you sell

A sale ends your eligibility for the head of family, veteran and valuation freeze benefits on that house, and the buyer's value is reset. Under Section 7-36-21.2, the three percent annual cap on residential value increases does not apply in the tax year after a change of ownership. The county values the home at current and correct value that year.

Factor this into your asking price and into what the buyer will pay afterward. A house you have owned for many years with a capped value can be reassessed upward for the new owner, even though your own bill was low.

Property tax is payable in two installments, November 10 and April 10, under Section 7-38-38. Unpaid tax draws interest of one percent a month starting thirty days after the due date.

Selling when creditors or liens are involved

If a judgment lien or unpaid debt is attached to your house, selling can be the cleanest way to deal with it, but the order of payment matters. Liens are paid from proceeds at closing in the order the title company finds them.

  • Pull a title report early so you know every recorded lien and its amount.
  • Confirm whether a judgment lien attached before July 1, 2023, since the exemption amount in force at that time may apply.
  • Ask a New Mexico attorney whether a claim of exemption should be filed before closing, particularly if a creditor has started execution.
  • Keep the property tax installments current so no tax lien rides along with the sale.
  • If the home is inherited and still in a deceased parent's name, resolve who has authority to sign before listing.

Cash Home Buyers works with owners in these situations and buys houses as they are, so repairs and showings are not part of the timeline. We are not a law firm, and nothing here replaces advice from a lawyer who knows your case.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the New Mexico homestead exemption in 2026?

It is $150,000, or $300,000 if the claimant's spouse died within two years before the claim and could have claimed it. The figures come from Section 42-10-9 as amended in 2023, effective July 1, 2023 for actions filed on or after that date.

Does the homestead exemption stop a mortgage foreclosure?

No. Subsection E of the statute says it does not apply to properly perfected liens of secured creditors or to garnishment. A mortgage you signed stays enforceable.

Do I have to apply to the county for the homestead exemption?

No. You assert it in the court case where a creditor is collecting, using the claim of exemption forms or your answer in a foreclosure. The county programs that reduce tax, such as head of family, are claimed with the assessor instead.

Are sale proceeds protected after I sell my home?

Not reliably. A 1991 bankruptcy decision held that proceeds of a voluntary sale are not exempt. Talk to an attorney before a sale if a creditor is pursuing you.

Can I claim the exemption on an inherited house?

Possibly. A 2020 bankruptcy decision allowed the exemption for an heir's undivided interest in an inherited house still titled in the deceased parents' names. The result depended on the heir's ownership interest and occupancy, so it is not automatic.

title: New Mexico Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling
content:
New Mexico Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Cash Home Buyers in New Mexico
Cash Offer in 24 Hours
  • New Mexico Estate and Inheritance Tax: inherited, behind on payments, tenants or repairs, we buy the house as-is
  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Mexico Estate and Inheritance Tax sale
  • Turn the New Mexico Estate and Inheritance Tax offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New Mexico House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in New Mexico?
We buy New Mexico houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Does New Mexico charge an estate tax?

In practice, no. The state's estate tax was phased out because of federal tax law changes as of January 1, 2005. The Estate Tax Act, Section 7-7-1 NMSA 1978 and following, is still on the books, and the Taxation and Revenue Department still asks for paperwork in one situation.

If the estate has to file the federal estate tax return, Form 706, for any reason, the personal representative also files a New Mexico return, form RPD-41058. When the department receives both, it issues a certificate of no tax due for the estate's records. The state due date is the federal due date, including any extension of time for the federal return.

The state tax equals the federal credit on the net estate. Returns and payments go to the New Mexico Taxation and Revenue Department, P.O. Box 25123, Santa Fe, NM 87504-5123. For help, call (505) 827-0763 or email Other.Taxes@tax.nm.gov.

No inheritance tax either

New Mexico does not impose an inheritance tax. Heirs who receive a house, cash or other property do not owe the state a tax for receiving it. With no estate tax in practice and no inheritance tax, the state itself takes nothing from the transfer.

When the federal estate tax applies

The federal tax reaches only big estates. The 2026 threshold is $15,000,000, which works out to a credit of $5,945,800 at 2026 rates, and most estates sit well under it.

Nine months after death, the federal return comes due. Some families file even with no tax owed, to elect portability of a deceased spouse's unused exclusion.

Taxes an heir may meet when selling an inherited New Mexico house
TaxDoes it apply to a New Mexico heir selling a house?
New Mexico estate taxPhased out as of January 1, 2005; a no-tax-due certificate is issued if a Form 706 was required
New Mexico inheritance taxNone
Federal estate taxOnly for estates above the exclusion, $15,000,000 for 2026 deaths
Income tax on estate earningsYes, if the estate or trust earns income; filed on form FID-1
Property taxYes; bills continue, and the lien runs from January 1
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Mexico house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Income tax on what the estate earns

An estate pays income tax on what it earns while it is open, at personal income tax rates. The state's fiduciary income tax return is form FID-1. This is a different tax from the estate tax, because it is based on income the estate or trust generates rather than on the value of what the decedent left.

A house sale during administration can generate gain. Keep the settlement statement, the date-of-death value and a record of repair and carrying costs, because the estate's accountant will need them.

Tax on gain when an heir sells

Heirs seldom owe much. For tax basis, inherited property is generally valued as of the owner's date of death. Filing or skipping an estate tax return does not change that. If the house sells close to that number, almost no gain shows up on your return.

When Form 706 was required, the basis must match the value finally reported on it. If no statement of that value ever reaches you, the appraised value at death used for state inheritance or transmission tax purposes can serve as the basis.

  • Book a date-of-death appraisal early, before repairs or cleanup alter the condition.
  • Collect the death certificate, the court's letters, and the deed or tax record showing how title was held.
  • Mention to the accountant any gift of the property to the decedent from you or your spouse within one year before death, since a different basis rule applies then.

Keep every closing document from the sale. Your accountant will want the settlement statement next to the appraisal. If several heirs share the house, each one reports a share of the sale, so agree early on who holds the paperwork and how proceeds will be split.

Probate and selling an inherited house

Most inherited houses go through probate before a sale. The deciding fact is how title is held. If only the decedent's name is on the title, probate is required. Joint tenancy, or a transfer on death deed that was recorded, lets the house bypass it.

The small-estate affidavit is a poor bet: it is limited to estates under $50,000 with no real property at all. A surviving spouse has one narrow route for the primary residence under Section 45-3-1205: at least six months must have gone by, no probate may be pending, and the assessed value cannot exceed $500,000, among other conditions. That affidavit is handed in at the clerk's office for the home's county.

Everything else starts with a probate case in the decedent's home county. The court fee is $30. A case can be opened anywhere from 5 days to 3 years after the death, and moving title may take a personal representative's deed. Past three years, probate is still possible when its only job is passing title to heirs.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Mexico houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Property tax during and after probate

Probate does not stop the tax clock. Each January 1 the year's real property tax attaches to the house as a first lien, outranking every other interest, and no paperwork is needed for that to happen. A bill nobody paid before the death is still owed afterward.

Value on a home normally cannot climb faster than 3 percent a year. A change of ownership removes that protection, with exceptions for a surviving spouse, for a child who occupies the house as a principal residence, and for certain revocable trusts in either direction. Suppose the heir in residence loses head of household status. The change of ownership is then deemed to happen in the first tax year after that.

An outside buyer starts with a reset value. Payments are due November 10 and April 10, and interest starts after December 10 and May 10.

Checklist before you list

First figure out who may sign. Then check the tax position.

  • Secure the probate court's letters, or confirm that a transfer on death deed or joint tenancy is already recorded.
  • Phone the county treasurer for the amount owed, including any bill left unpaid from an earlier year.
  • Ask the accountant whether a federal Form 706 or a state RPD-41058 is required.
  • Record any deed at the clerk's office. A deed left unrecorded does not affect title against a later purchaser.

Make those calls where the house sits. The title company can then pick a closing date and settle any tax balance from the proceeds. Heirs living far away often like a cash sale, since there is no buyer loan approval, no repair list and no repeated showings.

Frequently asked questions

Does New Mexico have an estate tax in 2026?

Effectively no. The state estate tax was phased out as of January 1, 2005. If a federal Form 706 is required, the estate also files form RPD-41058 and receives a certificate of no tax due.

Does New Mexico have an inheritance tax?

No. New Mexico does not impose an inheritance tax, so heirs owe the state nothing for receiving a house or cash.

What is the federal estate tax exemption for 2026?

The basic exclusion amount for 2026 deaths is $15,000,000. The return is due nine months after the date of death.

Do I need probate to sell an inherited house?

Usually, unless the house passed by joint tenancy or a recorded transfer on death deed. The small-estate affidavit does not cover real property, with a narrow spousal exception for a primary residence of $500,000 or less.

What is my tax basis in an inherited house?

Generally the fair market value on the date of death. A date-of-death appraisal is the usual proof.

What a quitclaim deed does

A quitclaim deed hands over whatever interest the signer has in a property, and nothing more. The short statutory forms in Section 47-1-44 NMSA 1978 show the difference. The warranty deed form ends with the words "with warranty covenants." The quitclaim form has no such line.

In outline, the quitclaim form says that for consideration paid, the grantor quitclaims to the grantee (whose address is stated) the described real estate in a named New Mexico county. A legal description follows, then the witness and seal line, then space for the acknowledgment. The statute text on Justia has the full forms.

When you sell a house, that missing promise is the whole story. A seller who signs a quitclaim isn't vouching that the title is clean, that nobody else owns a share, or that old liens were paid. The buyer gets the seller's interest and takes on the risk of everything else. Quitclaims therefore turn up mostly between relatives, after a divorce, when a name is added or removed, and when a boundary or a gap in the record needs cleaning up.

The county clerk can't tell you which form to use. The Santa Fe County Clerk's office, for one, is not bonded to advise whether a warranty deed, special warranty deed or quitclaim deed fits your situation, and suggests asking a real estate attorney.

Recording the deed and what it costs

Take the signed deed to the county clerk in the county where the property sits. The recording fee is $25 per document. Under Section 14-8-15 NMSA 1978, a clerk can't accept an instrument for filing until the fees are paid. Once a document has more than ten entries, another $25 applies for each extra block of ten or fewer entries added to the county recording index. Of each $25 fee, $18 goes to the county general fund and $7 to the clerk's recording and filing fund.

Counties add their own handling rules. Santa Fe County's are a useful sample of what to expect.

Recording fees and filing requirements
RequirementWhat appliesWhere it comes from
Base recording fee$25 for each document filed or recorded14-8-15 NMSA 1978
Large documentsAnother $25 for each added block of ten or fewer index entries beyond the first ten14-8-15 NMSA 1978
SignaturesOriginal signature and the notary's original signatureSanta Fe County practice
Notary blockMust be on the document, with a legible seal that doesn't cover signatures or printed textSanta Fe County practice
Electronic filingAvailable through Simplifile or CSC, which charge a convenience fee on top of recording feesSanta Fe County practice

Other counties may run things differently, so call the clerk where the house is. Santa Fe County's recording page shows the kind of detail clerks look for.

Spouses and quitclaim deeds

In most cases both spouses have to sign. Section 40-3-13 NMSA 1978 requires spouses to join in transfers of community real property, and in transfers of separate real property they hold together as joint tenants or tenants in common. If one spouse tries to transfer alone, the transfer is void, except that either spouse may transfer directly to the other.

There are two ways around it. A spouse can sign alone under a validly executed and recorded power of attorney, and a spouse who didn't join can later ratify the instrument in writing. Separate property owned by just one spouse can generally be transferred without the other's joinder.

If you're married and bought the house during the marriage, plan on two signatures.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Mexico house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

If the deed is never recorded

An unrecorded deed still binds the two people who signed it, but a later buyer who knew nothing about it can come out ahead. Under Section 14-9-3 NMSA 1978, an unrecorded deed doesn't affect the title or rights of a purchaser, a good faith mortgagee or a judgment lien creditor who had no knowledge of it.

  • Between grantor and grantee, an unrecorded deed is good, and it divests the grantor's title as between them.
  • In one quiet title case, a buyer who paid value in good faith and knew nothing of an earlier unrecorded deed won, even though the buyer's own paper was a quitclaim.

If a parent or former partner quitclaimed a house to you, record that deed before anything else. A sale can't close cleanly while the last deed in the chain sits in a drawer.

The assessor's affidavit

For residential property, usually yes. Section 7-38-12.1 NMSA 1978 requires whoever presents a deed for recording on residential property to also file an affidavit with the county assessor within thirty days of the date of filing with the county clerk. The transferor, the transferee or their authorized agents may sign it.

The affidavit covers only the names and mailing addresses of all transferors and transferees, the legal description, the full consideration paid or exchanged with the terms of the sale and any seller incentives, and the value and description of personal property included in the price. The assessor keeps the original as a confidential record, and it isn't part of the valuation record.

Many deeds are exempt. Among them:

  • A quitclaim deed to quiet title or clear boundary disputes.
  • An instrument between husband and wife, or parent and child, with only nominal actual consideration.
  • An instrument that confirms or corrects a deed already recorded.
  • A deed from a sale for delinquent taxes or assessments.
  • An instrument delivered to establish a gift or a distribution from an estate or trust.

The clerk sends the assessor a copy of every recorded document, but the person receiving the property is responsible for telling the assessor so the right person gets the tax bill. Unpaid property tax can eventually lead to a tax sale.

Tax sale deeds compared with quitclaim deeds

The deed the state issues after a delinquent tax auction is equivalent to a quitclaim deed. It conveys all of the former owner's interest as of the date the state's lien for real property taxes arose, subject only to perfected interests that existed before that date. New Mexico warrants no title to property sold at its auctions.

An interest is perfected when the deed or lien is recorded with the county clerk where the property is located. A buyer can use the tax deed as the starting point for clearing title through the court.

Grantees under a quitclaim deed from a tax sale purchaser take subject to defects they knew about, or that the record would have shown. The Taxation and Revenue Department's delinquent property tax auction page sets out the terms.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Mexico houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When a quitclaim works for a sale, and when it falls short

A quitclaim works when everyone understands that only the signer's actual interest is changing hands. It falls short when a buyer expects promises the form doesn't contain.

It usually works for:

  • Moving a house between family members who know the history of the property.
  • Removing a former spouse or co-owner who agrees to give up their share.
  • Passing along an inherited house where the heirs have settled who owns what, and the paperwork needs to catch up.

It usually falls short when:

  • The seller wants the buyer to rely on a promise that the title is free of claims.
  • Co-owners or a spouse haven't signed, so part of the interest never moved.
  • Liens, unpaid property tax or an old mortgage remain on record.
  • Someone with a claim, such as a tenant or relative, lives in the house and the deed doesn't address it.

A quitclaim can move an interest quickly, but it can't make a lien, a missing co-owner or a tax debt disappear. Those stay with the property, and a buyer's title review will find them. Cash Home Buyers doesn't promise a price in advance, and each New Mexico house gets looked at on its own facts.

Frequently asked questions

Is a New Mexico quitclaim deed the same as a warranty deed?

No. The statutory warranty deed form in 47-1-44 NMSA 1978 ends with warranty covenants, and the quitclaim form carries none. A quitclaim transfers only the interest the signer holds.

How much does it cost to record a quitclaim deed in New Mexico?

The fee is $25 per document under 14-8-15 NMSA 1978. An extra $25 applies for each additional block of ten or fewer index entries beyond the first ten. E-recording vendors add their own convenience fee.

Does a quitclaim deed have to be notarized?

For recording, yes in practice, since clerks look for a proper notary block. An acknowledgment isn't essential to a deed's validity between the parties, but an unrecorded deed can lose to a later good faith buyer.

Can one spouse sign a quitclaim deed alone in New Mexico?

Generally no for community real property. Section 40-3-13 makes a transfer by one spouse alone void, except a direct transfer to the other spouse. A recorded power of attorney or a later written ratification can change the result.

Do I file anything with the county assessor after recording a quitclaim deed?

Often yes for residential property. An affidavit is due to the assessor within thirty days of filing with the clerk under 7-38-12.1, unless an exemption applies, such as a quitclaim to quiet title or a transfer between parent and child for nominal consideration.

New Mexico Transfer on Death Deed: How It Works

Cash Home Buyers in New Mexico
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Mexico Transfer on Death Deed sale

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in New Mexico?
We buy New Mexico houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.

The law behind the deed

These deeds fall under 45-6-401 and the sections after it, New Mexico's version of the Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act. Section 45-6-405 NMSA 1978 boils the idea down: a person can name one or more beneficiaries to receive property when the person dies, and a transfer on death deed is how it's done.

The act started on January 1, 2014. Section 45-6-403 reaches deeds signed before, on or after that date, so long as the owner's death comes on or after January 1, 2014.

Under Section 45-6-404, other lawful ways to pass property stay open. You can still use a will, joint tenancy or a trust, and this deed simply adds another choice.

What the deed must contain

Three things make the deed valid under Section 45-6-409: it must look like a normal recordable deed, say the transfer happens at death, and be recorded while the owner is still alive.

  • Include everything a regular recordable deed between living people needs.
  • Say that the beneficiary receives the property when the owner dies.
  • Record it with the clerk of the county where the land lies before the owner's death.

Recording is the step people skip, and a signed deed left in a drawer accomplishes nothing. The county charges the fee set by 14-8-15 NMSA 1978: $25 per recorded document, plus extra for large documents with many index entries.

Section 45-6-410 drops several steps people assume are required. Nobody has to tell the beneficiary, hand over the deed, get the beneficiary's acceptance during the owner's life, or pay anything for it. An owner can sign and record without telling the person named.

What the owner can still do

Nearly everything. Section 45-6-412 says the deed leaves the owner's rights untouched during life, including the right to sell or pledge the property. After recording, you can still sell, refinance or borrow against the house.

Until the owner dies, the recorded deed has these limits on its reach:

  • a buyer's rights stay intact, even if the buyer knows about the deed;
  • creditors, secured or not and present or future, keep their rights;
  • neither side's eligibility for public assistance changes;
  • the beneficiary gets no legal or equitable stake;
  • the beneficiary's own creditors can't reach the property.

For a seller this is the important part. The beneficiary can't stop a sale and a buyer needs no signature from them. The deed matters only if the owner still holds the house at death.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Mexico house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Changing or revoking the deed

You need a new recorded document. Section 45-6-411 requires the owner to acknowledge the revocation after the acknowledgment on the original deed and to record it before death, in the same county clerk's office. It also has to be one of three types: a later transfer on death deed that cancels the first (directly or by conflicting with it), a stand-alone document that says it revokes, or an ordinary deed that says it revokes.

Shortcuts don't work. Ripping up a copy or scrawling across the deed does nothing once it's recorded. When several owners signed, one owner's revocation leaves the others' shares alone, and a deed by joint owners is revoked only if every living joint owner revokes.

The beneficiary's consent or knowledge isn't needed to revoke or amend, as long as the recording condition above is met.

What happens at the owner's death

When the beneficiary outlives the owner, the property goes to that person under the deed. Section 45-6-413 covers the details:

  • A beneficiary who dies first gets nothing, and that share lapses.
  • Multiple beneficiaries split the property into equal undivided shares, without survivorship rights between them.
  • If one lapses, the remaining beneficiaries divide that share in proportion to what each holds.
  • Where the signer co-owned the house and a co-owner lives on, survivorship gives the property to that co-owner. The deed takes effect only if the signer was the last joint owner standing.
  • Whatever is recorded against the house at death, whether conveyances, mortgages or liens, binds the beneficiary.
  • No covenant or warranty of title comes with the transfer, whatever the deed itself says.

In practice, the beneficiary records a copy of the death certificate with the clerk in the house's county, and title then passes with no probate.

Does the beneficiary owe the owner's debts?

In a limited way, maybe. Section 45-6-415 makes the beneficiary answerable for allowed claims against the owner's probate estate and for statutory allowances to a spouse and children, within the limits of 45-6-102 NMSA 1978.

The deed spares the house a probate case but doesn't shield it from debt. A mortgage stays on, and a beneficiary who wants to keep the house must keep paying it. Recorded liens follow the property, as 45-6-413 provides.

Property that passes automatically to a named beneficiary generally sits outside the probate estate, and land under a transfer on death deed is in that group.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Mexico houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Transfer on death deed versus other routes

Which route fits depends on how much control the owner wants.

Ways a house can pass at death
RouteHow it worksAuthority
Transfer on death deedRecorded while the owner lives; revoked only by a recorded document; beneficiary holds nothing until death45-6-409, 45-6-411, 45-6-412
ProbateOpened in the home county's probate court from 5 days to 3 years after death; $30 to fileCourt self-help guide
Small estate affidavitEstates under $50,000 with no real property, usable after 30 days if no probate is openCourt self-help guide
Personal representative's deedCan be required to take real property out of the decedent's nameCourt self-help guide

The court's guide at selfrepresentation.nmcourts.gov walks through probate in plain language, and the text of 45-6-413 is short enough to read in full.

Selling a house that has a transfer on death deed

The answer turns on whether the owner is living. A living owner sells as usual, since the deed puts no limit on transfers, and the sale closes on the owner's signature alone. If the owner sold before death, the deed has nothing left to transfer.

Once the owner has died, the beneficiary must first put ownership on record by filing the death certificate with the clerk. Only then can a sale proceed. The buyer's title search will turn up the deed, the certificate and any recorded liens. Because no warranty comes with the house, expect close scrutiny of title.

Inherited houses often need repairs, carry back taxes or belong to relatives who live far off. A cash sale can speed things up without changing the rules above. Cash Home Buyers makes no price promises in advance, and the beneficiary should check title steps with an attorney or title company before signing.

Frequently asked questions

Does a New Mexico transfer on death deed avoid probate?

For the house itself, yes. The beneficiary records the death certificate with the county clerk and title moves with no probate. Allowed claims against the probate estate can still reach the beneficiary under 45-6-415.

Must the deed be recorded before the owner dies?

Yes. Section 45-6-409 requires it to be recorded with the clerk of the property's county while the owner is alive.

Does the beneficiary have to be told about the deed?

No. Under Section 45-6-410, the beneficiary needn't be notified or accept anything during the owner's life, and no payment is required.

Can the owner sell the house after signing a transfer on death deed?

Yes. Section 45-6-412 leaves the owner free to sell or encumber the property, and the beneficiary has no legal or equitable stake until the owner dies.

What happens if the beneficiary dies before the owner?

That beneficiary's share lapses under 45-6-413. With several beneficiaries, the survivors divide the lapsed share in proportion to their interests.

New Mexico Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Cash Home Buyers in New Mexico
Cash Offer in 24 Hours

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a New Mexico Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale
  • Turn the New Mexico Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a New Mexico House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in New Mexico?
We buy New Mexico houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

How probate works in New Mexico

Probate here follows the Uniform Probate Code (Chapter 45 of the state statutes). You file in the county probate court for the place the person called home at death. Statewide there are 33 county probate courts next to 34 district courts.

Filing is open from 5 days to 3 years after death, at a cost of $30. If the person left a will, the court names whoever the will picks as personal representative (the executor), and the paper proving that power is Letters Testamentary. Without a will, the same power arrives as Letters of Administration.

Inherited a house? Start by asking who is allowed to sign the deed. That turns on how title was held and on whether a court has named anyone yet.

Houses that skip probate

Real estate held in joint tenancy, or covered by a recorded Transfer on Death Deed, moves without probate. A widowed spouse can also move a community property home that was titled solely to the late spouse, using an affidavit filed six months after the death.

The small estate shortcut rarely fits a house. It covers estates under $50,000 with no real property, where the successor collects assets by Affidavit of Successor in Interest after 30 days if nobody has opened a probate. Land, a house or a farm puts the estate outside that rule.

Whether probate is needed, by situation
SituationProbate needed?What happens instead
Estate under $50,000, no real propertyNoAffidavit of Successor in Interest after 30 days, signed and notarized
Home held in joint tenancyNoSurviving owner takes title
Home with a recorded Transfer on Death DeedNoNamed beneficiary takes title
Community property home in deceased spouse's name onlyNo, with affidavitSurviving spouse files six months after death
Home in the decedent's sole nameUsually yesThe personal representative may have to sign a deed as representative

Who can act as personal representative?

New Mexico sets a priority order for appointment in Section 45-3-203. Order of priority: the nominee in a probated will, then a spouse who is also a devisee, other devisees, the spouse, other heirs, and finally, once forty-five days pass after death, a creditor.

A person with priority may hand the role to another qualified person by filing a signed writing, and any adult may decline it. Minors can't serve, and neither can anyone a formal proceeding finds unsuitable. Objecting to an appointment requires a formal proceeding.

Siblings who inherit together sometimes disagree about who should serve, and that stalls everything. The court can decide, and no one should sign a sale contract before the appointment is final.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your New Mexico house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

What a personal representative does

The representative collects and lists the assets, tells the heirs, pays debts as far as estate money reaches, hands out what is left under the will or intestacy law, and closes the case. Closing takes a sworn statement that the work is done, and the case must stay open at least three months first.

The representative may not use estate funds for personal benefit but is entitled to fair compensation for time spent. Estate money can pay costs such as postage, filing fees and copies. Write down tasks and hours as you go.

  • Get your Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration before touching the house.
  • Locate the deed, mortgage statements and property tax bills.
  • Insure the property and pay its taxes for as long as the estate is open.
  • Log work and expenses so the court and heirs can see them.

Who owns the house during probate?

Under Section 45-3-101, at death, separate property and the decedent's share of community property go to those the will names, or to the heirs when there is no will. Case law on that statute holds that real estate goes straight to heirs or devisees rather than to the executor.

That ownership remains subject to administration, creditors and family allowances. A surviving spouse's half of community property is reachable by the estate until the claims period ends, and afterward only as needed to pay community debts.

When real property is in the estate, a Personal Representative's deed may be needed to take it out of the decedent's name. Drafting that deed is tricky, so use an attorney.

Creditor claims and your sale timeline

The representative can run a creditor notice once a week for three weeks in a general circulation newspaper in the county. Anyone owed money has four months from the first printing to file a claim or lose it, under Section 45-3-801.

Creditors the estate knows about can be notified directly, and their cutoff is whichever comes later: four months after publication or sixty days after delivery of the notice. The representative faces no liability for giving or skipping this notice, yet a 1977 decision found that publicizing the hearing on a final account did not reach known tort claimants.

Heirs planning a sale can use the claims period as a rough clock, since it lasts at least four months from first publication.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy New Mexico houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Can a personal representative sell the house?

Yes, as long as the will or a court order doesn't forbid it. Section 45-3-715 lets a representative who acts reasonably for the benefit of interested persons sell any asset, land in New Mexico included, for cash or on credit, publicly or privately.

It also covers repairs of any size, insurance, taxes and assessments, and leases that outlast the administration. When part of the price is financed, the unpaid balance must be secured unless the district court waives that for good cause.

  • A cash sale sidesteps the financing and security issue.
  • Selling as is saves the estate repair costs, which the law permits but doesn't demand.
  • Estate funds can cover taxes and insurance during the listing.
  • If the heirs disagree, a formal proceeding lets the court settle it.

Cash Home Buyers buys inherited houses in New Mexico as they are. We are not attorneys, and the personal representative should confirm authority with the estate's lawyer before accepting any offer.

Time limits and property tax during probate

Most probate proceedings, formal or informal, can't begin later than three years after death, with exceptions in Section 45-3-108 One exception allows a late appointment when nothing was filed in the three years, but then the representative's right to hold estate assets is limited and only administration expenses can be claimed.

Property tax keeps running during probate. Real property tax is a first-priority lien from January 1 of the tax year (Section 7-38-48). The bill is due in installments on November 10 and April 10, and late tax collects one percent monthly interest beginning thirty days past due.

Annual growth in a home's assessed value is capped at three percent, and a change of ownership resets the cap. The definition of that term in Section 7-36-21.2 leaves out certain transfers, such as one to a child who makes the house a principal residence. Selling to an outside buyer does count, so the buyer's bill may not match the estate's.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need probate to sell an inherited house in New Mexico?

Usually, when the decedent held the house alone. Joint tenancy and a recorded Transfer on Death Deed avoid probate, and a surviving spouse can use an affidavit for a community property home after six months.

What is the New Mexico small estate limit?

Under $50,000 with no real property. Owning a house puts the estate outside that procedure, so an Affidavit of Successor in Interest can't move it.

How long does probate take in New Mexico?

At minimum three months before closing. Creditors get four months from first publication to file claims, so plenty of estates run longer.

How much does it cost to open probate in New Mexico?

Filing costs $30. Lawyer fees, newspaper notice costs and the representative's pay are separate expenses the estate may owe.

What is the deadline to open a New Mexico probate?

You can file from 5 days to 3 years after death. Past three years, only limited proceedings remain, under Section 45-3-108.
